content.text: An exception in an endpoint doesn't crash an ASP.NET Core server; it ends that request. Register the exception handler once, at the top of the pipeline, with
, and every failure, including ones in endpoints nobody wrapped, becomes the same RFC 9457 response without leaking internals. Keep
for code that can actually recover.
The mobile team files a bug against the orders API: errors arrive in four shapes. The orders endpoints return

, payments returns a plain string, the newest endpoint returns an empty 500, and one response contains a full database error message, user and table names included. Every endpoint author handled errors. Each did it differently, and the one who forgot didn't handle them at all.
The belief: an exception that escapes an endpoint is a disaster, so every handler needs its own
that turns failures into a proper error response.
The instinct comes from good places. C# courses teach

as "error handling". In a console app, an unhandled exception really does kill the process. In Development, a failing endpoint shows a page full of stack trace, which looks like something users must never see. And in production, an endpoint that throws without any handler configured returns a 500 with an empty body, so wrapping the code seems like the only way to send something useful.
The last point is the real problem, and it has a better fix than a catch block in every endpoint.
An exception ends the request, not the server

When an endpoint throws, ASP.NET Core catches it around that request. The server logs it, the client gets a 500, and every other request carries on. Nothing crashes. The empty body is just what you get when nobody told the app how to describe errors.
One middleware at the top of the pipeline
that wraps everything registered after it, endpoints included. Combined with
, it catches any exception thrown further down, logs it, and writes a standard error response in place of the empty 500. Its partner,
, fills in error responses that have no body yet, such as a 404 from routing or a
. Because it guards only what comes after it, register the exception handler first.
ProblemDetails is a standard, not a Microsoft format
come from RFC 9457, which replaced RFC 7807. An error is a JSON object sent as
members, plus any extension members you add. ASP.NET Core adds a
extension. The RFC also advises against putting implementation details such as stack dumps in the response, which is exactly what
"Order not found" and "quantity out of range" are normal outcomes. Return them as results,
or a validation problem, and the problem details service shapes them like every other error. For exceptions you can't avoid but can classify, such as an EF Core concurrency conflict, write one
that maps them to a status code for the whole app.
